ev.c_h_quack.text.1: A trader at the market shouts that his potion cures fever, baldness, toothache and unrequited love. You didn't buy any, but you enjoyed listening - the show was better than any troupe of players.
ev.c_h_quack.text.1.E03: A trader at the market shouts that his potion cures fever, baldness, toothache and unrequited love. You didn't buy any, but you enjoyed listening - the show was better than the theater.
ev.c_h_quack.text.2: In the square a man in a motley cloak is selling powder of “ground horn from a wondrous beast” - for coughs, for the evil eye and for nagging neighbours. You didn't buy any, but you laughed till you cried.
ev.c_h_quack.text.3: A healer by the gate shows the crowd a jar with something dark floating in it - “drawn out of a merchant's belly”. Half the audience gasps, the other half clutches their stomachs. You left empty-handed and in excellent spirits.
ev.c_h_quack.text.4: At the fair a seller of back-ache ointment “cured” his limping helper so well that by evening the man was limping again - on the other leg. You laughed louder than anyone.
ev.c_h_quack.text.5: An old woman with a basket of roots swears her brew gave a singer back his voice, a shepherd his eyesight and a village headman his wits. The headman was standing right there, unsure whether to be offended. You bought nothing, but stayed to the very end.
ev.c_h_quack.text.6: A wandering tooth-puller works right in the market to the beat of a drum - so no one hears the screaming. Few patients, a huge crowd. You watched with a hand on your cheek, glad your own teeth are still sound.
ev.c_h_quack.text.7: By the well a foreigner has laid out dried lizards, feathers and bright pebbles - each one against its own ailment. You asked which one cures boredom. “Me,” he said, and did a trick with three nuts.
ev.c_h_quack.text.8: From his platform a trader drinks his own potion, gulp after gulp, to prove it's harmless. By evening he sits there pale and proving nothing at all. You went home without buying a drop, but with a story for the whole week.
ev.c_h_quack.text.9: A seller of “water of life” insists it's a hundred years old and he himself is two hundred. He looks about forty, but very tired. You listened, laughed and walked on without opening your purse.
ev.c_h_quack.text.10: On a rainy day under the market awning a healer is selling a cure for colds - and sneezing every other word. The crowd roars, he gets cross and sneezes again. You didn't buy any, but the day suddenly felt brighter.
ev.c_h_quack.text.11: Two traders at opposite ends of the square sell the same “one and only” cure-all and call each other frauds. You wandered from one to the other as if at a play, and bought nothing.
ev.c_h_quack.text.12: A man with a tame crow sells pills “against old age”: the crow, he says, pecks at them and has lived a hundred years. Just then the crow pecked his finger. You laughed and went on your way.
ev.c_h_quack.text.13: By the temple wall someone is selling “dust from the feet of a holy pilgrim” - a pinch at a time, good for everything. Judging by the amount, the pilgrim must have walked half the world. You bought nothing, but you were smiling till evening.
ev.c_h_quack.text.14: A village feast, and between the dances a travelling healer with magic oil: “Rub it on your brow and you'll grow wiser.” The local shepherd rubbed it on all over. You laughed so hard you nearly fell off the bench.
ev.c_h_quack.text.15: A trader shouts that his powder removes freckles, corns and debts. At “debts” the crowd perked up, and he raised the price on the spot. You didn't buy any, but you admired the nerve.
ev.c_h_quack.text.16: At the crossroads a healer's young helper gets muddled praising a remedy “for tooth fever and head baldness”. His master cuffed him; the crowd applauded. You walked away as pleased as if you'd been to a festival.
ev.f_omen_sky.text.1: In broad daylight the sun began to go dark, as if something were taking bites out of it. Dogs howled, birds fell silent, people dropped to their knees. A few minutes later the light returned - but what was it?
ev.f_omen_sky.text.2: The full moon rose over the rooftops - and began to darken until it was the deep red of dried blood. In the streets people banged on pots and shouted to scare off whatever was devouring it. By midnight the moon was bright again - but what was it?
ev.f_omen_sky.text.3: Every night a star with a long pale tail hangs over the rooftops like a broom. The old folk say such a star comes before war, plague or the death of a ruler. The neighbours whisper and glance at you: what do you think?
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.3: Say that tailed stars have come before and learned men wrote them down
ev.f_omen_sky.text.4: In the night the stars came pouring down - dozens, hundreds, one after another, as if someone were shaking the tree of heaven. Half the street is praying, half is making wishes. What does it mean?
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.4: Say the stargazers have seen this many times and no harm comes of it
ev.f_omen_sky.text.5: In the morning a pale ring formed around the sun, and two more suns lit up on either side - faint but clear. People in the market have dropped everything and are staring up. Someone is already shouting that it means three rulers at once.
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.5: Say it's only light playing in a cold haze, like a rainbow
ev.f_omen_sky.text.6: A ball of fire streaked over the fields, bright as day, and then came a crash that shook the walls. The boys are already running to find where the “sky stone” fell. The neighbours argue: is it heaven's anger or a good sign?
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.6: Say stones sometimes fall from the sky and wise men have held them in their hands
ev.f_omen_sky.text.7: For days now the sun has risen as a dull red disc - you can look straight at it without squinting. The air is hazy, as if half the world were burning somewhere far away. People are waiting for disaster and don't know what kind.
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.7: Say it's smoke or dust from far-off lands, not an omen
ev.f_omen_sky.text.8: In the night half the sky was flooded with red and green light, rippling like a curtain in the wind. Not even the old folk remember anything like it. Some say a distant land is burning; others, that heaven is opening its gates.
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.8: Say that in the far cold lands such lights are seen every winter
ev.f_omen_sky.text.9: A new star has appeared in the sky - brighter than all the rest, visible even by day. Yesterday it wasn't there. The learned keep quiet, the fortune-tellers argue, and in the market they're already selling charms “against the star”.
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.9: Say the stargazers have seen new stars before
ev.f_omen_sky.text.10: At noon the moon crept across the sun but didn't cover it completely: a ring of fire was left hanging in the sky. The light turned strange, shadows grew sharp, the hens went to roost. People froze in the middle of the street.
ev.f_omen_sky.text.11: Right in the middle of the festival the sun began to fade. The music broke off, someone dropped a dish, children started crying. A few minutes later the light returned, but no one could go on celebrating.
ev.f_omen_sky.text.12: A huge pale ring formed around the moon, with two false moons inside it. The dogs howled till morning. The woman next door insists it means a great death; her neighbour says a good harvest.
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.12: Say it's only light in a cold haze, like the ring around a lamp
ev.f_omen_sky.text.13: At sunset a bright star lit up right between the horns of the new moon, as if the moon were holding it. The fortune-tellers all agree it's a sign - they just can't agree of what. The neighbours wait to hear what you'll say.
ev.f_omen_sky.title.13: A Star in the Moon's Horns
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.13: Say the stargazers know the paths of the stars and this happens
ev.f_omen_sky.text.14: In the middle of the harvest the sun began to vanish, as if something were biting it away. The workers dropped their baskets and lay flat on the ground. A few minutes later the light returned, but the field stayed silent till evening.
ev.f_omen_sky.text.15: After a hot wind the rain came down - red as blood. The puddles are brown, and rusty streaks run down the white walls. People pray aloud and won't let the children out of the house.
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.15: Say the wind brought dust from distant deserts, that's all
ev.f_omen_sky.text.16: At dawn a pillar of light rose from the sun right up into the sky, as if someone had raised a column of fire. People are crowding into the square, arguing over who saw it first and what it means.
ev.f_omen_sky.explain.16: Say it's only light playing in a cold haze, like a rainbow
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.1: A lucrative job - but it means working on a holy day, when labour is a sin. The customer is in a hurry and pays double.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.1.christian: A lucrative job - but it means working on a Sunday, and a great feast day at that. The customer is in a hurry and pays double.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.1.islamic: A lucrative job - but it means working through the Friday prayer. The customer is in a hurry and pays double.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.1.jewish: A lucrative job - but it means working on the Sabbath. The customer, of another faith, doesn't see the problem, is in a hurry and pays double.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.2: A wealthy household is preparing a wedding and wants everything ready exactly for the festivities - which means on a holy day, when it's a sin to work. The steward promises double pay and taps his foot impatiently.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.3: The owner of the next field asks you to help bring in the harvest before the rains come. But tomorrow is a holy day, and the old folk are already giving you looks. He pays double - the rains won't wait.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.4: A travelling merchant sets off at dawn after the feast and needs the goods ready. That means working straight through the holy day. He lays double pay on the table.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.5: An old craftsman in the next quarter has died; the funeral is the day after the holy day, and everything must be ready beforehand. It means working on the feast; his family pays double and begs you not to refuse.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.6: The wind tore the roof off the shopkeeper's place across the street, and he'll pay double to have it covered before the next storm. Only tomorrow is a holy day, and working on it is a sin.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.7: A nobleman wants a gift for the feast and won't wait. The work would fall right on the holy day - and he is not a man who likes to hear “no”. He pays double.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.8: The mistress of a great house orders a mountain of festive food and wants it hot, on the holy day itself. Kneading dough on a feast day is a sin, but she pays double.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.9: A trader wants his stall and awning mended for the fair, and the fair opens the moment the holy day ends. You'd have to work on the feast. He's in a hurry and promises double.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.10: Someone's goods must be carried and stacked before the city gates close for the feast. The owner pays double, but you'd be hauling sacks on the holy day while all decent folk go to pray.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.11: A craftsman you know is behind on a big order and calls you in to help: it means working on the holy day, but the pay is double and he'll never forget it. He looks at you hopefully.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.12: Half the street wants something new for the feast, and the last orders arrive on the very eve. To finish in time you'd have to work on the holy day itself. They'll pay double - as long as it's done.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.13: The town steward has ordered the gates repaired for the feast, and there aren't enough hands. You're offered double pay to work on the holy day, while all decent folk are at prayer.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.14: The fruit in a neighbour's orchard has all ripened at once and is about to drop. The owner is calling for workers on the holy day and pays double - tomorrow will be too late.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.15: The customer is a foreigner of another faith: to him the holy day is an ordinary working day, and he can't see the problem. The job pays well - double - but you'd be working on the feast.
ev.f_holy_day_work.text.16: A neighbour whispers: on the holy day the streets are empty, no one will see, and the job is urgent and pays double. A sin, of course. But it's good money.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.1: Grandfather carved you {g:a little wooden horse on wheels|a wooden doll with jointed arms}. Now you sleep hugging it and drag it everywhere all day.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.2: The carpenter next door whittled you {g:a horse with a real mane of tow|a doll in a little scrap-of-cloth headscarf} from offcuts. You won't let go of it even at meals.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.3: Grandmother sewed you {g:a little rag horse with fruit-stone eyes|a rag doll with a braid of yarn}. You carry it everywhere and whisper secrets to it.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.4: An old groom from the big house carved you {g:a galloping horse with a rider|a foal with a ribbon round its neck}. Every evening now you “water” it by the door from a potsherd.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.5: The potter at the market made you {g:a clay horse whistle|a little clay horse whistle with a painted mane} and wouldn't take any payment. Now the whole yard knows when you're home: the whistling carries three streets away.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.6: Grandfather made you {g:a hobby horse - with a head, a mane and a bridle|a little cart with a horse to pull your doll around}. You race about the yard with it till dark and refuse to go to bed.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.7: A pedlar gave you {g:a wooden horse with a chipped ear|a little doll with only one shoe} for helping carry his basket. You think it's the finest thing in the world and put it to bed beside you.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.8: The big kids on the street made you {g:a little straw horse tied up with string|a straw doll wearing a wreath}. It's lopsided, but you wouldn't trade it for anything.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.9: A shepherd, killing time, carved you {g:a horse that tosses its head when you pull a string|a doll that nods when you pull a string}. You pull the string all day long and never tire of it.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.10: An old soldier from the next street carved you {g:a warhorse with a shield hanging from the saddle|a little rider doll on a tiny horse}. You play at going on campaign and trumpet loudly into your fist.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.11: A carver at the fair gave you {g:a little horse on wheels|a painted doll} - just because you stared at it for so long with such admiration. You still can't believe your luck.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.12: Grandfather whittled by the hearth all evening, and in the morning beside your bed stood {g:a team - two little horses and a wagon|a tiny cradle with a doll and a horse to pull it}. You squealed loudly enough to wake the whole street.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.13: Your nurse twisted together {g:a little horse with a horsehair tail|a doll with horsehair hair} out of thread and wood chips. Now you put it to bed before you go to bed yourself.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.14: The old harness-maker stitched you {g:a little horse in real harness|a doll in leather slippers, with a horse to match} from leather scraps. Now you have the finest toy in the whole quarter, and you walk about with your nose in the air.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.15: After the rain you and Grandfather shaped {g:a whole herd of little clay horses|a clay doll and a horse for her} and dried them in the sun. One cracked, but that's the one you love best.
ev.y_wooden_toy.text.16: Grandfather gave you {g:a wooden rocking horse|a doll riding a little horse} and told you he'd had one just like it as a boy. You didn't leave its side all day.
ev.a_house_fever.text.1: The summer was stifling, and one after another the whole household fell ill. The fever shakes you every other day, as if on schedule.
ev.a_house_fever.text.1.rome: The summer was stifling, damp air drifts up from the low ground by the river, and one after another the whole household fell ill. The fever shakes you every other day, as if on schedule; no wonder the Romans built altars to the goddess Fever herself.
ev.a_house_fever.text.2: The autumn turned out warm and damp, the ditches are brimming, and in the evenings clouds of mosquitoes whine over them. A week later the whole household is in bed: fever, chills, fever again - every other day, as if on schedule.
ev.a_house_fever.text.3: The floodwater went down, but the puddles stayed - a little marsh in every yard. Soon the fever was going through the house: one moment you're shaking so hard your teeth chatter, the next you're burning like an oven.
ev.a_house_fever.text.4: An acquaintance from far away stayed the night on his journey - and a few days later his illness was making the rounds of the house. Everyone fell ill one after another; the fever comes back every other day.
ev.a_house_fever.text.5: The city is sweltering, the streets smell of rot, and the stench from the ditch under the windows gets through any curtain. One after another the whole household fell ill - fever, chills, delirium at night.
ev.a_house_fever.text.6: There was a reason the new house was cheap: there's a bog behind it, and at night a damp mist creeps up from it. By midsummer there wasn't a healthy soul left in the house.
ev.a_house_fever.text.7: The fever is working its way down the street house by house, and now it has reached yours. You lay listening to the neighbours coughing through the wall - and then all your household went down too.
ev.a_house_fever.text.8: The summer was warm and rainy, and stagnant water stands in every barrel and potsherd. First one fell ill, then a second, then you too. The fever comes and goes like the tide.
ev.a_house_fever.text.9: At night you're woken by a rattling - it's someone in the house whose teeth are chattering with chills. By morning, fever; by evening, chills again. Within a week the whole house was down.
ev.a_house_fever.text.10: After the great festival half the town came down with fever, and your house is no exception. Everyone is laid up side by side, and there's no one to fetch water.
ev.a_house_fever.text.11: The stream ran low this year and turned green, and a heavy smell hangs over it at night. The fever started in the houses by the bank and reached yours: everyone is down.
ev.a_house_fever.text.12: Right at the busiest time of the harvest the whole household fell ill one after another - no one even to bring water, let alone work. The fever strikes every other day, as if it knows when people can least spare the time.
ev.a_house_fever.text.13: The fever you know from years past is back: once again everyone in the house is burning and shaking, once again the neighbours leave soup at the door. The old folk say it will come every summer now.
ev.a_house_fever.text.14: No one remembers a summer with so many mosquitoes: they whine day and night, and no smoke keeps them off. Then one after another the household fell ill - fever, chills and aching bones.
ev.a_house_fever.text.15: The nights are so stifling that everyone sleeps out in the yard - and evidently they shouldn't have: by the end of the month the fever had laid out the whole house. It shakes you every other day, regular as counting.
ev.a_house_fever.text.16: First the strongest person in the house fell ill, and everyone was surprised. Then the rest went down too, and there was no one left to be surprised. The fever makes the rounds of the beds every other day, like a mistress inspecting her house.
ev.v_dice_first.text.1: Behind the tavern, by the light of a single lamp, men are throwing dice. The stakes are small, the laughter loud, and they make room for you on the bench.
ev.v_dice_first.text.1.rome: Behind the popina, out of the aediles' sight, men are throwing dice: gambling for money is banned in Rome except at the Saturnalia, but who cares? They make room for you on the bench.
ev.v_dice_first.text.2: Under an awning at the fair, among the sacks and baskets, traders are hard at dice. One shifts over and nods at the space beside him: “Want a throw?”
ev.v_dice_first.text.3: The guards at the city gate are passing the night with dice by torchlight. They recognise you and call out: “Come on, one throw - for luck!”
ev.v_dice_first.text.4: At a wedding, once the elders have gone to bed, the young people bring out the dice. The stakes are laughable, but everyone's eyes are shining. Someone hands you the cup.
ev.v_dice_first.text.5: In the back room of the workshop, once the master leaves, the apprentices throw dice on an upturned crate. Tonight, for the first time, they've invited you.
ev.v_dice_first.text.6: At the roadside inn, drovers and travellers throw dice by the hearth late into the night. The stakes are modest, the stories loud, and someone is already shifting over to make room for you.
ev.v_dice_first.text.7: On the festival night, behind the temple wall and away from stern eyes, people are throwing dice. Laughter, little lights, the clink of stakes - and someone slaps you on the shoulder: sit down.
ev.v_dice_first.text.8: While the mill grinds your grain, the men waiting their turn are throwing dice right on a sack of flour. There's nothing else to do anyway - they make room for you.
ev.v_dice_first.text.9: Under the old bridge, by a little fire, some cheerful types are throwing dice. The dice clatter on the stone, the lamp smokes. “New here? Sit down, we play small.”
ev.v_dice_first.text.10: At a wealthy acquaintance's house, after supper the guests are brought dice and a carved cup. The stakes are different here, and so is the laughter - quiet. The host nods you to an empty seat.
ev.v_dice_first.text.11: The rain drove everyone indoors at the eating-house, and soon dice were rattling on the table. Someone is already staking his last pennies, someone else is winning his back. They push a bench your way.
ev.v_dice_first.text.12: The market has closed, but the traders haven't gone home: a game of dice has started on an empty stall. They call you over to join, as one of their own.
ev.v_dice_first.text.13: In the midday heat, in the shade at the edge of the field, the workers have brought out dice and are throwing them on a spread-out shirt. “Have a go - maybe you'll be rich by evening!”
ev.v_dice_first.text.14: A grey-haired old man at the eating-house is teaching the young ones to throw dice “properly” - and beating every one of them. He winks at you: “Go on, your turn.”
ev.v_dice_first.text.15: It's a festival, the streets are full of lights, and on every corner someone is shaking dice in a fist. A neighbour presses a pair into your hand: “Everyone's lucky tonight!”
ev.v_dice_first.text.16: The travellers have stopped for the night by the road, and dice appeared by the fire straight away. The stakes are whatever's in each man's purse. They make room for you on the log.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.1: Every night the woman next door carries bread to an abandoned shed. You peeked: a runaway slave is hiding there, hardly more than a boy. Sheltering runaways is punished harshly - and so is knowing about it.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.2: Every evening the old potter from your street lowers a basket of food into the dry well beyond the village. You followed him: a runaway slave is sitting down there - thin, his feet torn and bleeding. Those who shelter runaways are punished severely, and so are those who knew and kept quiet.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.2: Nobody noticed. A week later the well was empty: he had climbed out - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.3: Every morning the washerwoman from the next yard carries a basket down to the stream - and not just with laundry in it. A runaway slave is hiding in the reeds by the water, very young. You saw him. Sheltering runaways is punished harshly - and so is knowing about it.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.3: Nobody noticed. A week later the reeds were empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.4: Playing among the old tombs outside the village, you noticed someone hiding in one of the burial vaults - a runaway slave with a brand on his shoulder. And that evening the girl from next door crept there with a bundle of food. You know what happens to those who shelter runaways, and to those who keep silent.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.4: Nobody noticed. A week later the vault was empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.5: The baker from the next street, always so sullen, carries flatbreads up to his loft every night. You peeked: a runaway slave is hiding there - young and frightened. Those who hide runaways are punished severely, and so are those who knew.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.5: Nobody noticed. A week later the loft was empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.6: In a haystack in the far field you found a man asleep - a runaway slave, hardly more than a boy. He woke, saw you and just put a finger to his lips. One of the neighbours is already bringing him water - you saw the tracks. Sheltering runaways and keeping quiet about them are punished alike.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.6: Nobody noticed. A week later the haystack was empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.7: Every evening the old shepherd climbs to the cave on the hill with a bundle - far too big for one man. You crept after him: a runaway slave is hiding inside. Sheltering runaways and staying silent about them are punished equally harshly.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.7: Nobody noticed. A week later the cave was empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.8: At night a little light flickers in the ruins of a burnt-out house. You crept closer: a runaway slave is hiding there, and someone has already left him a jug of water and some bread. You know what happens to those who shelter runaways - and to those who stay silent.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.8: Nobody noticed. A week later the ruins were empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.9: The boy next door, your constant playmate, made you swear an oath and took you to the old byre: a runaway slave is hiding there, very young. Your friend has been sneaking him food for three days. If anyone finds out, everyone who knew will be punished.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.9: Nobody noticed. A week later the byre was empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.10: In the night you heard the woman next door creeping towards the abandoned workshop with a bundle. In the morning you looked in: a runaway slave is hiding behind a pile of old baskets. Sheltering runaways is punished harshly - and so is knowing about it.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.1: Nobody noticed. A week later the workshop was empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.11: Under the old bridge, in a dry niche above the water, a runaway slave is hiding - you saw him when you climbed down after a dropped toy. That evening the old market woman went down there too, with flatbreads. Those who hide runaways are punished harshly, and so are those who knew.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.1: Nobody noticed. A week later there was no one under the bridge - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.12: The herb-woman at the edge of town is nursing someone in her storeroom: you spotted bloodied rags and a shadow behind the curtain. It's a runaway slave, still very young, and hurt. Sheltering runaways is punished harshly - and so is knowing about it.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.1: Nobody noticed. A week later the storeroom was empty - as soon as he could stand, he slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.13: Someone is hiding in the shared granary outside the village: every morning you found footprints and crumbs by the door. It turned out to be a runaway slave, and the young widow from the end of the street is secretly bringing him food. Helping runaways is forbidden on pain of punishment - and so is knowing and keeping quiet.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.1: Nobody noticed. A week later the granary was empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.14: In the ravine behind the houses, in an old clay pit, a runaway slave is sitting - just a boy; he's twisted his ankle and can't get away. You've seen the girl next door running down there with flatbreads. Helping runaways is forbidden on pain of harsh punishment - and so is knowing and saying nothing.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.1: Nobody noticed. A week later his ankle had healed and the pit was empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.15: Someone is living on the flat roof next door, under an awning of mats: you've seen eyes peering out. The old woman who owns the house, a quiet soul, carries food up there when everyone's asleep. It's a runaway slave - and sheltering runaways is punished harshly, and so is keeping quiet.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.1: Nobody noticed. A week later the roof was empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.y_runaway_secret.text.16: A runaway slave is hiding in the grove beyond the village, where the grown-ups go only on feast days. You stumbled on him while gathering firewood, and fresh bread lay beside him - so one of the neighbours is already feeding him. Sheltering runaways is a grave crime, and so is knowing and saying nothing.
ev.y_runaway_secret.bring_food.success.1: Nobody noticed. A week later the grove was empty - he had slipped away in the night.
ev.first_love.text.1: You keep thinking about one person. Say something, or stay silent?
ev.first_love.text.2: Every morning at the well you meet the same person - and every time you drop your bucket. The neighbours are starting to snigger. Maybe it's time to say something?
ev.first_love.text.3: At the festival you ended up side by side in the dance, and since then you can't think of anything else. The festival is over, but your heart is still dancing. Say something, or stay silent?
ev.first_love.text.4: You work side by side all day, and you catch yourself waiting for morning just for that. One glance and everything slips from your hands. Confess?
ev.first_love.text.5: Someone sings by the water in the evenings, and you'd know that voice among a thousand. Today you finally saw whose it is. Go over and tell them?
ev.first_love.text.6: On long evenings the young folk gather round one hearth - sewing, weaving, chattering. You sit where you can see one particular face, and don't hear a word of the conversation. Confess?
ev.first_love.confess.success.6: The feeling was mutual. You will remember those evenings by the hearth forever.
ev.first_love.text.7: This morning there was a flower on your doorstep, and you're almost sure who left it. You think about that person all day. Speak first, or wait?
ev.first_love.confess.success.7: The feeling was mutual. And the flower, it turned out, was no accident. You will remember this summer forever.
ev.first_love.text.8: At harvest you worked the same row, and at noon you shared one flatbread between you. Ever since, you've been dreaming of that field. Say something, or stay silent?
ev.first_love.confess.success.8: The feeling was mutual. You will remember this autumn forever.
ev.first_love.text.9: At the neighbours' wedding everyone was watching the couple, and you were watching one of the guests. All evening you kept catching each other's eye across the yard. Go over and tell them?
ev.first_love.text.10: A new family moved into your quarter, and since then you've been walking past their house far too often. One face at the window gives you no peace. Confess?
ev.first_love.text.11: At the market there's someone behind one particular stall from whom you now buy everything - even things you don't need. Soon the whole house will be buried in onions. Say something - or keep buying onions till you're old?
ev.first_love.text.12: Everything is blooming this spring, and you go about in a daze, sighing. Only you know the reason - and, it seems, half the street. Confess?
ev.first_love.confess.success.12: The feeling was mutual. You will remember this spring forever.
ev.first_love.text.13: You slipped on the wet steps, and someone's hands caught you. That was a week ago, and you still remember those warm palms. Say something, or stay silent?
ev.first_love.text.14: You grew up on the same street, fought, made up, climbed trees together - and suddenly you see this person in a completely different way. You're afraid of ruining everything. Confess?
ev.first_love.text.15: In the temple, in the festival crowd, you see one face - and find yourself praying for something quite other than you should. Now at every feast your eyes search for it. Tell them?
ev.first_love.text.16: A downpour drove the two of you under the same awning. You talked about nothing, laughed, and then the rain stopped far too soon. You can't forget that hour. Tell them?
ev.y_knucklebones.text.1: You won a whole handful of knucklebones from the neighborhood kids. The secret is simple: throw with a twist and hold your breath.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.1.E03: You won a whole handful of knucklebones from the neighborhood kids. The secret is simple: throw with a twist and hold your breath.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.1.rome: You won a whole handful of knucklebones from the neighborhood kids. You rolled the Venus throw - all four showing different sides! - and even the older boys came over to look.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.2: You won a whole bag of nuts from the neighbourhood kids: you aim one nut at a little pile of three - and never miss. Now nobody wants to play with you, but your pockets are full of nuts.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.3: You bet you could walk along the very top edge of the old wall - and you did. The prize: the best flat skimming stone in the neighbourhood. Your knees only started shaking afterwards.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.4: At pebbles - toss one up and snatch the rest off the ground - you beat the whole street. The secret is simple: watch the stone, not your opponent.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.5: You won a spinning top from the older kids, staking your best stick-sword on it. Risky - but the top is yours now, and it hums louder than any other.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.6: They roll clay marbles towards a hole by the wall - and today every last marble rolled your way. You strutted down the street with your pockets clinking like a rich man's.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.7: The kids were arguing over who could throw a stone furthest across the stream. You threw - and took the whole prize: a handful of bright beads and a feather.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.8: You staked your only knucklebone on a single throw - and swept the whole pile. The older kids checked for tricks, but there weren't any: just luck.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.9: At odds-and-evens you guessed right seven times in a row. The boy next door sulked, but handed over the dried fruit he'd lost fair and square.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.10: You bet the other kids you could climb the tallest tree on the street. Up, down - and a clay whistle for your prize. Plus a couple of scratches thrown in.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.11: You played pick-up sticks: whoever pulls out the most without moving the others wins. Your hands don't shake - and the whole pile is yours now.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.12: You won a bet that you wouldn't blink while the others counted to a hundred. Your eyes watered, but the prize was worth it - a handful of knucklebones as white as teeth.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.13: You were tossing fruit stones into a jar from five paces. You got nine out of ten and carried home a whole handful of beads you'd won.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.14: You risked everything you owned - three knucklebones and a pretty feather. You won ten times over. Now you're sure that luck loves the bold.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.15: The other kids were teaching you a new game - tossing pebbles into squares scratched in the dirt. By evening you'd beaten your teachers and taken all their pebbles.
ev.y_knucklebones.text.16: You were playing knucklebones on the temple steps until someone chased you off. You'd already won two handfuls and were the first to scarper.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} challenged you to arm-wrestling - and won. You said you let {g=npc_sex:him|her} win. No one believed it, including you.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} challenged you to a race to the well - and got there first. You said you were saving your strength. Apparently your knees were saving theirs too.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.3: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} easily lifted a sack you can barely shift. You acted as if that was the plan all along and went off to rub your back. You're proud - of {g=npc_sex:him|her}, and just a little of yourself.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} beat you at a board game for the first time - and not by luck: three times running. You demanded a fourth game. You shouldn't have.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.5: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} split twice as much firewood as you without even getting out of breath. You explained that your axe was blunter. The axes were identical.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.6: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} set you a riddle, and you wrestled with it all evening. The answer was so simple that you grumbled till bedtime - and glowed with pride.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.7: You were throwing stones to see who could go furthest. Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} beat you by a good ten paces and generously offered you “another go”. You declined - with dignity and an aching shoulder.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.8: At the market your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} haggled a price you'd never have dared dream of. The trader looked at you with sympathy. You acted as if you'd taught {g=npc_sex:him|her} that yourself.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.9: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} brought two full jugs back from the well while you carried one and stopped twice for a rest. “Need a hand?” {g=npc_sex:he|she} asked. You had no answer.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.10: You wrestled on the grass like in the old days, when {npc} was tiny. Only this time you were the one pinned flat. Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} helped you up - gently, as if you were an old {g:man|woman}.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.11: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} can whistle through two fingers loud enough to send the birds flying off the roof. You tried to do the same and only sprayed everyone around you. The whole house laughed all evening.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.12: You bet on who could climb the old tree in the yard fastest. {npc} was already at the top while you were still looking for a handhold. From above came: “Take your time, mind your back!”
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.13: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} talked you into a mock stick-fight - and knocked the stick out of your hand on the third blow. You said the sun was in your eyes. It was evening.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.14: You set out to test whether {npc} could do sums in {g=npc_sex:his|her} head - and a minute later you were the one counting on your fingers. Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} waited with angelic patience.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.15: Whoever got their bundle of firewood home first would be the winner. The winner was {npc}. You arrived after, puffing, and announced that what matters isn't speed but neatness.
ev.c_teen_wrestle.text.16: You challenged your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} to arm-wrestling, sure you'd win. {npc} won - left-handed, and without stopping chewing. You haven't brought it up since.
ev.f_m_easter.text.4: On Holy Saturday you helped decorate the church with branches and the first flowers. And at night, when the candles were lit, it seemed to you that every flower was glowing by itself.
ev.f_m_easter.text.5: The bells had been silent for three days, and on Easter morning they all rang out at once. You ran out into the street, and the whole town was ringing like one great bell.
ev.f_m_easter.text.6: Easter morning: strangers in the street embrace you and say “Christ is risen!” You answered “He is risen indeed!” so many times that by noon you were hoarse.
ev.f_m_easter.text.7: You carried a basket of Easter food to the church to be blessed. On the way home the basket felt lighter and the sun brighter than ever before.
ev.f_m_easter.text.8: The procession around the church at midnight: hundreds of little flames moving through the dark, and everyone singing. You walked in the crowd and felt part of something vast and good.
ev.f_m_easter.text.9: At Easter you made peace with a neighbour you hadn't spoken to for a whole year. He held out his hand first - “it's the feast, after all.” You took it, and your heart felt light.
ev.f_m_easter.text.10: The Easter bread rose tall with a golden-brown top, and the neighbours came round to admire it. You broke off the first piece after the service and decided nothing in the world tastes better.
ev.f_m_easter.text.11: On Easter night the church was so packed that candles stood on the windowsills and on the steps. You were right by the doors, but the singing reached you even there - and it seemed the most beautiful thing in the world.
ev.f_m_easter.text.12: At Easter you took some festive food to a lonely old woman at the end of the street. She cried, then laughed, and blessed you three times. You walked home smiling at everyone you passed.
ev.f_m_easter.text.13: Easter dawn: the service was over, and everyone went out to greet the sun. They say that on this day it dances for joy. You watched - and you think you really saw it.
ev.f_m_easter.text.14: After the Easter service the whole street turned into a party: songs, treats, children with rattles. You ran about with everyone else until dark, and nobody scolded.
ev.f_m_easter.text.15: Easter came after a long, hungry spring - and still everyone laid the table as best they could. You looked at the neighbours, the candles, the bread, and thought: poor is poor, but a feast is a feast.
ev.f_m_easter.text.16: On Easter evening the old folk sat outside the church remembering the Easters of their childhood. You listened till dark and realised that one day you'll be telling the very same stories.
ev.c_amulet.text.1: {npc} now wears a charm against the evil eye. You spent longer choosing it than you once spent choosing a {g:wife|husband}.
ev.c_amulet.text.1.egypt: {npc} now wears an Eye of Horus in blue faience, against sickness and the evil eye. You spent longer choosing it than you once spent choosing a {g:wife|husband}.
ev.c_amulet.text.1.rome: {npc} now wears a {g=npc_sex:bulla, the round charm a Roman boy takes off only when he becomes a man|lunula, the little silver crescent a Roman girl takes off only before her wedding}. You spent longer choosing it than you once spent choosing a {g:wife|husband}.
ev.c_amulet.text.2: {npc} sleeps with a red thread round {g=npc_sex:his|her} wrist - against the evil eye. The oldest woman on the street tied it, muttering words nobody else knows. You felt calmer at once.
ev.c_amulet.text.3: {npc} wears a blue eye-bead round {g=npc_sex:his|her} neck: let the evil eye look at the bead and not at the baby. You and your {g:wife|husband} argued about the colour of the bead for three evenings.
ev.c_amulet.text.4: A string of little bells now hangs over the cradle: if an evil spirit creeps near, they'll ring. {npc} reaches for them and laughs, and you hear every jingle even in your sleep.
ev.c_amulet.text.5: {npc} now wears a little pouch of herbs, blessed at the temple, round {g=npc_sex:his|her} neck. It smells so strong that evil spirits must flee three streets away. You're at peace.
ev.c_amulet.text.6: {npc} wears an animal's fang on a cord - to grow up brave and keep every sickness away. Where you got it from, better not to ask.
ev.c_amulet.text.7: A little knot of salt and charcoal is now sewn into the swaddling - the neighbour women recommended it. {npc} knows nothing about it and sleeps sweetly, while you've checked the knot four times today.
ev.c_amulet.text.8: {npc} wears a pebble with a hole through it, found by the stream: they say water itself bores such stones against misfortune. You spent half a day crawling along the bank looking for it, and you regret nothing.
ev.c_amulet.text.9: The wise woman whispered over the cradle for a long time and hung a bunch of dried herbs at its head. {npc} sneezed - and she said that was good: the evil was coming out.
ev.c_amulet.text.10: {npc} now wears a little carved guardian figure. The carver swore it protects against fever, the evil eye and night terrors. You believed him - you very much wanted to.
ev.c_amulet.text.11: Your {g:wife|husband} insisted that {npc} wear a charm round {g=npc_sex:his|her} neck, as children always have in {g:her|his} family. At first you smirked; now the first thing you do each morning is check it's still there.
ev.c_amulet.text.12: {npc} came back from the temple with a blessed charm round {g=npc_sex:his|her} neck and slept all the way home. It seemed to you that even the house had grown quieter and brighter.
ev.c_amulet.text.13: {npc} wears a bracelet of beads on {g=npc_sex:his|her} ankle - one from every neighbour who came to offer congratulations. The beads are all different, the thread is shared. You reckon no evil could stand against a guard like that.
ev.c_amulet.text.14: You spent the whole evening carving a tiny wooden charm - a bit crooked, but your own. Now {npc} gnaws on it with toothless gums, and you're sure that makes it work even better.
ev.c_amulet.text.15: {npc} now sleeps under an embroidered canopy: they say its pattern confuses evil spirits so they can't find their way to the baby. You stared at the pattern so long that you got lost in it yourself.
ev.c_amulet.text.16: The neighbours gave so many charms that {npc} jingles at every move like a travelling pedlar. You kept just one - the simplest, from the old woman next door. The rest hang on the wall, just in case.
ev.c_visit_old.text.3: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} brought a pot of stew made from your own recipe. It came out better than yours. You said it needed more salt - and ate two bowls.
ev.c_visit_old.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} sat with you on the doorstep all day, listening to the old stories - the same ones {g=npc_sex:he|she} knew by heart as a child. And didn't interrupt once. You noticed.
ev.c_visit_old.text.5: When the cold came, your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} brought you a thick warm blanket and tucked you in - the way you once tucked {g=npc_sex:him|her} in. You grumbled that you weren't a child - and were asleep within a minute.
ev.c_visit_old.text.6: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} took you to the market “just for a stroll” and bought everything you so much as glanced at. You scolded the whole way home - and carried your new things as carefully as a baby.
ev.c_visit_old.text.7: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} mended the sagging fence, chopped the firewood and only then sat down to eat. You watched and wondered: when did {g=npc_sex:he|she} become so capable?
ev.c_visit_old.text.8: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} brought up again the idea of you moving in with {g=npc_sex:him|her}. Again you said no. But it was nice to be asked - and the two of you talked till dark.
ev.c_visit_old.text.9: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} brought the first fruit from {g=npc_sex:his|her} own garden and watched you taste it for a long while. “Is it good?” {g=npc_sex:he|she} asked, exactly as {g=npc_sex:he|she} used to at five.
ev.c_visit_old.text.10: No sooner had you started coughing in the street than by evening your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} was at your door with herbs and a stern face. You'll cough more carefully from now on - and with pleasure.
ev.c_visit_old.text.11: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked you for advice - real advice, about something that mattered. You'd thought nobody asked you anything any more. You talked for half the day, and you felt ten years younger.
ev.c_visit_old.text.12: At the feast your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} sat you in the place of honour and let no one interrupt you. You told the same story three times, and everyone laughed all three times.
ev.c_visit_old.text.13: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} came round for no reason at all, and the two of you sat side by side in silence, watching the sun go down. Sometimes that's the best conversation there is.
ev.c_visit_old.text.14: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} scrubbed your floors, cleaned out the hearth and rearranged everything {g=npc_sex:his|her} own way. You spent three days hunting for your spoon - and smiled every time you found something in the wrong place.
ev.c_visit_old.text.15: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} found {g=npc_sex:his|her} childhood toy in an old chest and brought it round: “Remember this?” You did. You laughed and reminisced until late into the night.
ev.c_visit_old.text.16: In a downpour your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} ran across half the town to check that your roof wasn't leaking. It wasn't. {g=npc_sex:He|She} stayed till morning anyway - “since I'm here.”
ev.c_figs.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} came home with a lap full of the neighbor's fruit - and the neighbor right behind, holding the little thief by the ear and demanding justice.
ev.c_figs.text.1.E03: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} came home with a lap full of figs - and the neighbor right behind, holding the little thief by the ear and demanding justice.
ev.c_figs.text.1.athens: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} came home with a lap full of figs - and the neighbor right behind, holding the little thief by the ear and demanding justice. They say that's why Athenian informers are called sycophants - "fig-showers".
ev.c_figs.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} spent half a day up the neighbour's tree: the dog below wouldn't let {g=npc_sex:him|her} down. Now the neighbour stands at your gate with the dog, the little thief and a shirtful of evidence - demanding justice.
ev.c_figs.text.3: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} was doing a brisk trade in choice fruit on the corner - until the neighbour came by and recognised his own crop. Now he's on your doorstep, holding the young trader by the ear and demanding justice.
ev.c_figs.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} proudly handed you a basket of ripe fruit - “a present!” Before you could even be touched, the neighbour knocked at the door: the present, it turns out, grew in his orchard. He demands justice.
ev.c_figs.text.5: Every child on the street has sticky hands and a happy face today: {npc} was generously handing out the neighbour's fruit. The neighbour counted his losses and marched the generous little thief to you by the ear - demanding justice.
ev.c_figs.text.6: In the night the neighbour heard branches snapping in his orchard and caught a small shadow with a shirt full of fruit. It was {npc}. He's brought the little thief home by the ear and demands justice.
ev.c_figs.text.7: “They just fell!” insists {npc}, clutching an armful of the neighbour's fruit. The neighbour, holding {g=npc_sex:him|her} by the ear, insists they fell after someone gave the tree a good shake. He demands justice.
ev.c_figs.text.8: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} volunteered to help the neighbour with his harvest - and carried half of it home down {g=npc_sex:his|her} shirt. The neighbour noticed, gave chase, and now holds the little helper by the ear, demanding justice.
ev.c_figs.text.9: A whole gang of children raided the neighbour's orchard, but only {npc} got caught - shirt bulging, face sticky. The neighbour holds {g=npc_sex:him|her} by the ear, lists the accomplices and demands justice.
ev.c_figs.text.10: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} came home in a torn shirt with a shirtful of fruit: a scrap of the shirt was left on the neighbour's fence. The neighbour followed - the scrap in one hand, the little thief's ear in the other - demanding justice.
ev.c_figs.text.11: {npc} picked the neighbour's fruit to take to a sick old woman at the end of the street. A kind heart - but someone else's orchard. The neighbour holds the kind-hearted thief by the ear and demands justice.
ev.c_figs.text.12: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} gorged on the neighbour's unripe fruit and is now groaning and clutching {g=npc_sex:his|her} belly. The neighbour stands there and evidently thinks that isn't punishment enough: he demands justice.
ev.c_figs.text.13: {npc} swapped {g=npc_sex:his|her} little knife with the other kids for a basket of fruit - without asking where it came from. It came from the neighbour's orchard, and he's already at your gate, holding the little swapper by the ear and demanding justice.
ev.c_figs.text.14: The neighbour, who wouldn't give you so much as a windfall, caught your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} in his orchard with full hands. {npc} swears {g=npc_sex:he|she} only picked up what was lying on the ground. The neighbour is counting every single fruit and demanding justice.
ev.c_figs.text.15: Before the festival {npc} decided to decorate your table - and did: with a mountain of the neighbour's fruit. The neighbour recognised his crop through the window, came in, caught the little thief by the ear right by the table and demands justice.
ev.c_figs.text.16: The neighbour put a scarecrow in his orchard, but your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} dressed it in {g=npc_sex:his|her} own shirt and calmly picked fruit while the neighbour chased the “thief”. The trick came out. Now the neighbour holds the real thief by the ear and demands justice.
ev.c_grand_story.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} asked about your youth. With every retelling the story gains more bandits, storms and heroics. Soon you'll believe it yourself.
ev.c_grand_story.text.2: {npc}, your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter}, won't go to sleep without a story, and you make up a new one every evening. Tonight it had a talking tortoise, a foolish giant and you yourself. {g=npc_sex:He|She} fell asleep at the best part - and you never found out how it ended.
ev.c_grand_story.text.3: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} corrects you at every turn: “Last time there were three bandits, not five!” You have to remember your own inventions - harder than any heroics.
ev.c_grand_story.text.4: You taught your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} a song from your own childhood. Now {npc} sings it all down the street, getting the words wrong, and the neighbours ask where such an antique came from.
ev.c_grand_story.text.5: {npc}, your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter}, asked: “Were you really little once?” So you had to tell about your childhood - including the time you fell into a ditch full of ducks. Now that story is demanded every evening.
ev.c_grand_story.text.6: By the fire {npc} listens to tales of the monster that lived across the river when you were young. Every evening the monster grows bigger, toothier and hungrier. Tonight your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} asked for the lamp to be left burning.
ev.c_grand_story.text.7: {npc} retold your story to the neighbours' children - so well that now you single-handedly defeat a whole army in it. The children look at you with respect. You didn't set them straight.
ev.c_grand_story.text.8: {npc} climbed onto your lap and demanded a story “about the scariest thing”. You told about a storm you once lived through out in the fields. In the story the storm lasted three days; in truth it was over by lunch.
ev.c_grand_story.text.9: In the evening {npc}, your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter}, asks you to tell “how it was in the old days”. You describe a time when everything was cheaper, people were more honest and summers were hotter. {g=npc_sex:He|She} listens open-mouthed and seems to believe every word.
ev.c_grand_story.text.10: {npc} found an old trinket of yours and asked where it came from. The story took the whole evening and featured a long road, a cunning merchant and a night under the stars. About half of it was true.
ev.c_grand_story.text.11: {npc}, your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter}, never takes {g=npc_sex:his|her} eyes off you as you tell how you first earned your own bread. In the story you did in one day what really took a month. {npc} promises to grow up exactly like you.
ev.c_grand_story.text.12: {npc} asked for a story, and you'd forgotten the ending. You had to make one up on the spot, and it came out so well that now your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} wants only that one - and only with that ending. Which you no longer remember.
ev.c_grand_story.text.13: At bedtime you told your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} about the time you got lost in a strange town when you were young. {npc} listened holding your hand, as if you might get lost right there and then.
ev.c_grand_story.text.14: {npc}, your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter}, invented a game: you tell the story while {g=npc_sex:he|she} acts out every character in turn. The bandit was especially good - the whole house laughed till they had hiccups.
ev.c_grand_story.text.15: Sitting by the fire, you told your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} about the stars - what they were called when you were young and the stories told about them. Now {npc} knows the sky better than you and quizzes you every evening.
ev.c_grand_story.text.16: {npc} asked whether you'd ever been afraid. You meant to laugh it off, and then told the truth - about real fear and how you got the better of it. {g=npc_sex:He|She} listened in silence, and hugged you tighter than usual when saying goodnight.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.1: The dog you once fed as a puppy has gone grey around the muzzle. Tonight he suddenly started barking furiously: someone is breaking into the storeroom.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.2: The old dog sleeps all day these days and is hard of hearing. But tonight he was the first one up, growling as he hasn't since he was young: strange voices are whispering by the granary.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.3: Your dog's legs barely carry him now, but his nose is as keen as ever. In the middle of the night he whined at the door, then started barking: someone is climbing over the fence into the yard.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.4: A rainy night, everyone asleep. Only the old dog you took in as a puppy stands by the gate, hackles raised, growling low into the dark. Over by the storeroom someone is fiddling with the lock.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.5: On the festival night, while the whole street sleeps off the celebrations, your old dog started barking. You looked out: two men are dragging sacks out of the shed.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.6: The dog has grown old, deaf in one ear, and spends most of his time by the hearth. But tonight he suddenly rushed to the door: someone is moving about in the workshop, and it isn't you.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.7: The old dog woke you by pushing his cold nose into your hand - and immediately growled towards the yard. Shadows are flitting by the cellar, and there's whispering.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.8: Night, moonlight, silence - and suddenly the hoarse bark of your grey old dog. Someone has already got into the vegetable garden and is hastily stuffing everything ripe into a sack.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.9: Your dog - the very one you once fed by hand - no longer gets up to greet visitors. But he still knows a stranger: in the middle of the night he burst out barking, and someone is working at the bolt on the granary door.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.10: On this moonless night even the crickets were quiet. The half-blind old dog raised his head, sniffed the air and dashed for the storeroom, barking as you haven't heard him bark in years.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.11: You were up late, the old dog dozing at your feet. Suddenly he sprang up, hackles raised: through the wall, in the shed, something thumped and someone swore under his breath.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.12: All evening the old dog was restless, wouldn't eat and kept watching the road. In the night you understood why: two strangers who'd been hanging about the gate by day are breaking into your storeroom.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.13: On a cold night the old dog was asleep, curled up on the doorstep. Suddenly he lunged growling into the dark: someone is rustling sacks by the grain store.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.14: Your dog has gone completely grey and hasn't barked even at cats in ages. All the more alarming, then, his barking tonight: two men are standing at the storeroom door with a lamp hidden under a cloak.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.15: While you slept, the old dog went out into the yard and lay down by the storeroom - as if he knew. Before dawn he raised such a racket that you jumped up barefoot: the door is ajar and someone is inside.
ev.y_dog_saves.text.16: You'd long since accepted that the dog was a useless watchman now: he sleeps, grunts, sighs. But tonight he's barking and straining towards the shed, and a shadow with a sack on its shoulder is darting out of it.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.1: A warm wall, the sun, a cool drink and nothing to do until evening. You never knew a person could live like this.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.1.E03: A warm wall, the sun, a cup of watered wine and nothing to do until evening. You never knew a person could live like this.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.1.JPN: A warm veranda, sunshine, a cup of warmed sake and nothing to do until evening. You never knew life could be like this.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.2: You sit on the bench by the gate and watch life go by: water-carriers, traders, children, dogs. No one expects anything of you. So this, it turns out, is happiness.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.3: In the morning you stepped out onto the doorstep and simply stayed there: sun on your face, birds in the branches and not a single thought of work. Once you'd have called it laziness. Now you call it wisdom.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.4: In the shade of the old tree by the well gather people just like you - grey-haired and in no hurry. You talk about the weather, prices, young people these days. Time moves on; you don't.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.5: On a cool day you found the warmest spot against the wall in the whole neighbourhood and sat there till noon, squinting like a lizard on a stone.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.6: You toss crumbs to the birds and watch them squabble over each one. All your life you were rushing somewhere, and the most interesting things, it turns out, were happening right at your feet.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.7: The children from the next yard are playing right at your feet, and instead of shooing them away you give them tips. The sun warms your back; the day stretches out slow and sweet.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.8: After lunch you dozed off in the shade of the awning, and when you woke the sun was already sinking. No one had woken you, no one had come looking. You stretched and decided that life had turned out well.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.9: Warm rain drums on the awning, and you sit beneath it with a hot drink, listening to the noise of the street. Nowhere to hurry to. You never knew rain could be so cosy.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.10: You carried a stool out into the sun and sat fiddling with some trifle - just to keep your hands busy. People you knew walked past and nodded. You nodded back, and nothing more was needed.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.11: In the evening you sit by the door and watch the sky change colour - gold to pink, pink to blue. There never used to be time for this. Now there is, and it's the best thing you have.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.12: The young people in the street argue, rush about, quarrel over nothing. You watch them from your bench, warming yourself in the sun, and smile: you've been through all of that, and now you can simply watch.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.13: You settled under a tree in the garden, where the bees hum and the warm earth smells sweet. You did nothing for half a day - and didn't feel guilty once.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.14: You have your own spot at the market now - on the step of an old friend's stall. You don't buy or sell anything, you just sit, chat and watch the crowd. The best show in town - and free.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.15: You sat by the water with your feet in the cool and watched the current carry the leaves away. Not a single task until evening. You never imagined life could be like this.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text.16: Morning sun, a bowl of something warm in your lap and a chat with the neighbour over the fence - about nothing and everything. The chores can wait. For the first time in years you don't have to be anywhere.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.1: You lost a tooth. The boy next door said to throw it onto the roof; Grandmother said to bury it by the threshold. Just in case, you hid it in a crack in the wall.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.2: The tooth had been wobbling for a week and came out when you bit into a stale flatbread. You studied it on your palm for a long time and decided you were nearly grown up now.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.3: The boy next door tied a thread to your wobbly tooth and the other end to the door. The door slammed, you squealed, the tooth flew. It hurt less than it scared you.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.4: You threw your fallen tooth over the roof, as the woman next door told you to, and asked the mouse for a new, strong one. Now every morning you check with your tongue to see if it's growing.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.5: The tooth fell out in the street in the middle of a game, and the whole gang spent half the day crawling in the dust looking for it. Found it! You carried it home in your fist like a jewel.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.6: Now there's a gap in your mouth, and it's perfect for whistling through. You whistle from morning to night, and the whole street is already longing for the new tooth to grow in.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.7: Grandfather pulled out your wobbly tooth in one go while you were looking at a bird that wasn't there. It's annoying to have been tricked - but the tooth is already in your hand, and it didn't hurt at all.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.8: You lost a tooth, and the older kids said you should give it to a dog - then the new ones would grow in strong like a dog's. The dog wouldn't eat it. You hid it in a crack by the doorstep - just in case.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.9: You boasted to the other kids that you'd already lost three teeth and they hadn't lost any. They counted. It was two, but you still won.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.10: Grandmother said to bury the fallen tooth under a tree, so the new ones would grow strong as roots. You buried it and ran to check every day whether anything had sprouted.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.11: The tooth fell out straight into your bowl of stew. You fished it out with a spoon to roars of laughter and proudly showed it to everyone until evening.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.12: In the morning you found the tooth on your sleeping mat. The woman next door said it was a good sign and gave you a sweet cake for it. You're already wiggling the next one with your tongue.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.13: Without your front tooth you lisp, and the word “sunshine” comes out funniest of all. The other kids make you say it again and again. At first you were hurt, then you started laughing along.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.14: You tossed your tooth onto the roof and asked: “Crow, crow, take my old one, give me a new one!” The crow flew past without answering - you decided that meant “yes”.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.15: The tooth had been loose for so long that you'd grown used to it, like a friend. When it came out you were even a little sad - and then you put it with your most precious things: a pebble, a feather and a bead.
ev.y_lost_tooth.text.16: The old woman next door said a fallen tooth must be thrown in the fire so evil spirits can't find it. You threw it in - it crackled, and you ran off in fright. But now the spirits certainly won't get it.
ev.c_law.text.1: A neighbor has gone to court: your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc}, he says, broke a jug over his head at the tavern. {npc} swears the neighbor started it. Half the tavern saw it, and each tells a different story.
ev.c_law.text.2: A neighbour has gone to court: your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc}, he says, knocked down his fence one night and trampled his whole vegetable plot. {npc} insists the fence fell by itself and {g=npc_sex:he|she} only went in after a runaway dog. The neighbours are split down the middle.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.2: The neighbour got enough for a new fence - enough for a fortress wall. The case was dropped.
ev.c_law.patron.success.2: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The neighbour suddenly recalled that the fence had been wobbly for ages.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.2: The court ordered a fine and a month's work in the neighbour's garden. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.3: There was a brawl at the fair, and a merchant from the next town is pointing at your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter}: {npc}, he says, overturned his stall and smashed all his goods. {npc} says {g=npc_sex:he|she} was trying to break up the fight. The merchant demands a trial and compensation.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.3: The merchant got more for his goods than he'd have made at the whole fair. He withdrew the complaint with a smile.
ev.c_law.patron.success.3: Your acquaintance whispered in the right ear, and the merchant suddenly remembered it was someone else entirely who knocked over the stall.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.3: The court ordered a fine and a month's work for the merchant - hauling his goods. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.4: A neighbour's shed burned down, and he swears the fire spread from the bonfire {npc} and friends were sitting round that evening. {npc} swears the fire was stamped out long before. The neighbour demands a trial and damages.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.4: The neighbour got enough for a new shed - better than the old one. The case was dropped.
ev.c_law.patron.success.4: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The neighbour suddenly recalled leaving a lamp burning in the shed himself.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.4: The court ordered a fine and a month's work building the new shed. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.5: A great man's servant complains that {npc}, in front of the whole market, called his master a thief and doused the servant himself with slops. {npc} says the bucket fell by itself and the words were the plain truth. The matter has gone to court.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.5: The servant was paid for his ruined clothes and his hurt feelings - twice over. He stopped feeling hurt at once.
ev.c_law.patron.success.5: Your acquaintance sorted it out behind the right doors: the servant was told to forget about the bucket.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.5: The court ordered a fine and a month's work in that same great man's courtyard. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.6: At the festival {npc} was wrestling in the ring and broke an opponent's nose. The injured man's family has gone to court: they say the throw was foul. {npc} insists it was all by the rules, and the witnesses, as usual, are arguing themselves hoarse.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.6: The injured man was paid so much he seems ready to break his nose again. The case was dropped.
ev.c_law.patron.success.6: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The injured man's family suddenly admitted the throw was fair.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.6: The court ordered a fine and a month's work for the injured man's family. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.7: A shopkeeper is taking it to court: {npc}, he says, took goods on credit and never paid a penny. {npc} swears it was all paid back in front of witnesses - only now the witnesses can't remember a thing.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.7: The shopkeeper got his “debt” back with such interest that he bowed to the ground. The case was closed.
ev.c_law.patron.success.7: Your acquaintance paid the shopkeeper a visit, and the man suddenly remembered the debt had been repaid back in the spring.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.7: The court ordered the debt repaid and a month's work for the shopkeeper. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.8: A neighbour has lodged a complaint: the dog {npc} keeps bit him in the middle of the street. {npc} claims the neighbour hit the dog with a stick first. Half the street saw it, and they're all on different sides.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.8: The neighbour got enough for his treatment - enough for three such legs. The case was dropped.
ev.c_law.patron.success.8: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The neighbour suddenly recalled stepping on the dog's tail himself.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.8: The court ordered a fine and a month's work for the neighbour. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.9: A neighbour is accusing your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter}: {npc}, he says, dug through the ditch one night and diverted all the water onto your field. {npc} says the rain washed the ditch out. It's gone to the judge, and half the village is coming to look at the ditch.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.9: The neighbour got so much for the “stolen water” that it could have flooded half the village. The case was dropped.
ev.c_law.patron.success.9: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The neighbour suddenly agreed that the rain really had washed the ditch out.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.9: The court ordered a fine and a month's work - clearing the neighbour's ditch. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.10: A potter has gone to court: {npc}, on a dare, jumped over his stall and smashed fifty pots. {npc} insists the stall was standing in the middle of the road. The witnesses are laughing, and each tells a different story.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.10: The potter was paid for his pots as if they were painted vases. He withdrew the complaint and even invited you to drop by.
ev.c_law.patron.success.10: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The potter suddenly recalled that the pots were cracked already.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.10: The court ordered a fine and a month's work for the potter - kneading clay. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.11: The innkeeper claims {npc} left without paying for three nights and suppers - and took a blanket too. {npc} says {g=npc_sex:he|she} paid in full and the blanket was a gift. It has gone to court.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.11: The innkeeper was paid for three nights, the suppers and the blanket - three times over. He withdrew the complaint.
ev.c_law.patron.success.11: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The innkeeper suddenly found his blanket in a cupboard.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.11: The court ordered a fine and a month's work at the inn. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.12: There was a fight with the watch at the city gate last night, and the guards swear {npc} started it. {npc} says {g=npc_sex:he|she} only stood up for a friend. The case has gone to the judge.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.12: The guards were paid “for their treatment and their pride”. They promptly forgot who started the fight.
ev.c_law.patron.success.12: Your acquaintance had a quiet word with the captain of the watch, and the case was quietly closed.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.12: The court ordered a fine and a month's work repairing the town wall. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.13: The herd {npc} was minding wandered into a rich neighbour's field and ate half his crop. {npc} insists the hedge was full of holes. The neighbour demands a trial and compensation.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.13: The neighbour was paid for his crop as if it were three years' harvest. The case was dropped.
ev.c_law.patron.success.13: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The neighbour suddenly admitted the hedge had needed mending for ages.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.13: The court ordered a fine and a month's work in the neighbour's field. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.14: A wealthy townsman is accusing your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter}: {npc}, he says, threw a stone that smashed his shutters and his favourite jug along with them. {npc} swears someone else threw it. The witnesses keep contradicting each other.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.14: The townsman got enough for new shutters and a new jug - carved ones, better than before. The case was dropped.
ev.c_law.patron.success.14: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The townsman suddenly decided the wind had broken his shutters.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.14: The court ordered a fine and a month's work in the townsman's yard. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.15: A former friend is accusing your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter}: in a quarrel over a game, he says, {npc} broke his arm. {npc} says the man fell off the bench all by himself. The witnesses only remember that it was loud.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.15: The former friend got enough for his treatment - enough for three such arms. The case was dropped.
ev.c_law.patron.success.15: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The former friend suddenly recalled that he'd fallen off the bench himself.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.15: The court ordered a fine and a month's work for the injured man. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
ev.c_law.text.16: A market woman has lodged a complaint: {npc}, she says, deliberately knocked over her baskets of eggs and laughed about it. {npc} insists {g=npc_sex:he|she} just tripped. Half the market saw it - and half the market is arguing.
ev.c_law.pay.ok.16: The market woman was paid for her eggs as if they were gold. She withdrew the complaint and promised to pray for you.
ev.c_law.patron.success.16: The influential acquaintance had a word in the right ear. The market woman suddenly recalled that her baskets were right in the gangway.
ev.c_law.answer.ok.16: The court ordered a fine and a month's work for the market woman - carrying her baskets to market. {npc} worked it all off - and barely spoke to you.
